title: Published Government Cash Surplus Numbers and Impact on Government's Fiscal Space and Decision on GST Rate Increase
what_it_is: Published Government Cash Surplus Numbers and Impact on Government's Fiscal Space and Decision on GST Rate Increase

sections.label: Cash surpluses and GST increase
sections.summary: A question asks whether published cash surpluses show more fiscal space and reduce the need for the planned GST increase, noting cash receipts differ from spendable revenue.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
sentences.text: asked the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (a) whether the Government’s published cash surpluses indicate that the Government has more fiscal space than it states in its Budget Statements; and (b) whether this reduces the need for the planned increase in GST rate.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
sentences.text: There is a distinction between (a) cash receipts and (b) revenue that is available for spending.

sections.label: NIRC as revenue source
sections.summary: The NIRC is now the largest single source of Government revenue, supporting about one-fifth of spending needs.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
sentences.text: The NIRC is now the largest single source of Government revenue, supporting about one-fifth of our spending needs.

sections.label: Land sales cash surpluses
sections.summary: Most cash surpluses come from land sales proceeds, which do not create additional revenues and are not a valid reason to delay the GST increase.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
sentences.text: The bulk of our cash surpluses arise from land sales proceeds.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
sentences.text: Such cash proceeds do not create additional revenues for the Government and are therefore not a valid reason for holding off the GST increase.

sections.label: Drawing $11 billion for COVID-19
sections.summary: This year, the first full financial year of this term, the President's approval was sought and obtained to draw up to $11 billion against COVID-19.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: And that is exactly what we have done this year because we have been facing one of the biggest crises of all.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: This year, the first full financial year of this term of government, we sought and obtained the President's approval to draw up to $11 billion for the continued fight against COVID-19.

sections.label: Deficit of $11 billion
sections.summary: A social media post said the deficit should be $3.5 billion, but the Government expects a deficit of $11 billion this year and has explained why.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: In their social media post, what they had actually said was that: "the Government says that the Government expects a deficit of $11 billion" and they said the deficit should only be $3.5 billion.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: The Government has set out the correct fiscal position.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: We do expect in this year, a deficit of $11 billion and we have explained why.

sections.label: GST and Assurance Package
sections.summary: GST is one option, with 60% of revenue from tourists and higher income, and a $6 billion Assurance Package buffers Singaporeans against the increase.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: So, GST is one of the options that we have, but because we know that GST does have an impact on the lower income and the vulnerable, we take steps to deal with that.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: So, as the Deputy Prime Minister explained earlier, actually 60% of our GST revenue comes from tourists and from the higher income.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: But we do know that middle income and lower income are affected, which is why we set aside the $6 billion Assurance Package, which will effectively buffer the majority of Singaporeans for five years against the increase and the lower income for 10 years.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: And with respect to the last question, I think, whether when we look at our reserve position – we have already explained all of that in the Budget statement and Round-up speeches; it is not necessary for me to go into that.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: But essentially, our formula for spending of the returns is a fair one – 50% of returns.

sections.label: Past constitutional reserve amendments
sections.summary: The passage recalls past constitutional amendments in 1991, 2001, 2008 and 2015 that introduced and extended reserve protection and NIR frameworks.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
sentences.text: And if you look at, I recall Minister Lawrence Wong mentioning in 2018 that, we should never say never.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
sentences.text: So, if you look at the past amendments to the Constitution that we have done: in 1991, this was when the reserve protection framework was introduced; in 2001, we had the Net Investment Income framework; in 2008, NIR framework; and in 2015, Temasek Holdings was included the NIR framework as well.

sections.label: Returns split 50-50
sections.summary: The last amendment encapsulated the formula of using 50% of returns for now and 50% for later.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: The last amendment really encapsulated the formula that we want to use, the principle, which is that, on the returns, we use 50% for now, 50% for later.

sections.label: GST Voucher and fiscal position
sections.summary: The passage states the permanent GST Voucher Scheme will be enhanced when GST rises, and rejects the suggestion that cash surpluses mean the fiscal position is better or GST need not rise.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: Do not forget we have also said that we will enhance the permanent GST Voucher Scheme when the GST rate is raised.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: This will provide a permanent cushion for lower and middle income households, even after the temporary support ends.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: So, it has been thought through very carefully, understanding that there is an impact on middle income and lower income, but we have taken the steps to ameliorate that, to buffer that, to make sure that they are okay.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: But this still brings me back to the point I started off with, which is that it is not correct to suggest that because, we have a certain amount of cash surpluses that we therefore, that our fiscal position is better than we have stated or that we do not need to raise GST.
